wake.title: and he does
body:
You sit down in your own chair, at your own desk, on the split trestle you have been meaning to see to since before the water — and the leg takes your weight the way it has taken it for eleven years, which is to say it holds, because there is something folded under it that is holding.

You put your hands on the machine.

The keys are worn. All of them, evenly, in the way of a machine that has been used rather than owned — except one in the top row, which is worn shinier than the rest, down past the lettering to the metal.

It is the O.

There is a bowl of something soft at Chef D.'s that has been telling you so for a fortnight, three or four times a night, in onion, on a plate, sent out to the room to be eaten by strangers.

You finish the sentence.

It takes four words and none of them are clever, which is a relief, because you have spent eleven years being clever in a town that was built out of it and it has not once been the thing that was needed.

Behind you the room does not do anything dramatic. There is no light and no wind. There is simply, at some point in the middle of the fourth word, one fewer person standing in a nine-by-eleven room, and the chair he was behind is where it was, and it is still pushed back, and it is going to stay pushed back now.

Silvora Reefs stops.

Not violently. The way a thing stops being the case when nobody is putting it: the green lamps do not go out, they were never lit, and the harbour was never wet, and the fog that never quite cleared did not clear because it was a clause in a sentence somebody has now stopped writing.

Darek Dwayne Wayne, who drove down to a slipway at four in the morning, has the cone made before the bell over the door has finished. And then he does not, and then there is no bell, and then there is no door.

You wake up.

It is an ordinary room and it is not nine feet by eleven. It is not any number by any number; nobody has measured it and nobody is going to, and the corners are where corners are and they will be there tomorrow.

There is a window in it. There is weather behind the window and the weather is doing what weather does, which is nothing in particular, unbeautifully, without a front coming through the lounge at ten and without anybody's voice changing on the word sky.

Your watch is on the table.

It says twenty past six. And it is going — the second hand is going, sweeping, arriving somewhere and leaving it — and the going is the part you cannot stop looking at, and you look at it for a very long time before you get up.

consequences.text:
There is a can on the table by the watch.

It is sealed, and it is labelled in a hand that is not yours, in careful capitals by somebody who wanted it legible to a stranger — *Third of March, NEARLY* — and it has held. Whatever is in it is still in it. You have picked it up four times this week and you have not opened it and you are not going to, and the not-opening is the entire point and always was.

You get up. You go to the window.

Somewhere below there is a road, and there is no ice cream on it, and there is no truck pulled onto the verge at four in the morning with the keys still in it. Nobody on that road is sorry about your wait. Nobody on that road has ever been sorry about anything on your behalf, and that is what an ordinary road is, and you stand there for a while getting used to it.

At six o'clock, out of the habit of a fortnight, you say good evening to a piece of empty air.

The air is empty. It stays empty for the whole of the pause you leave for an answer, which is longer than a pause has any business being.

And you do it again the next day, at six, in an ordinary room with weather behind the window — and the day after that — and it is some weeks before you stop, and you never quite decide to.

The desk in this room is a desk.

It has four legs and they were made as legs, by somebody who made desks, and it stands level on an ordinary floor. Not one of them is split. There is nothing folded and grey wedged into any of them, and there is nothing to take out and read, and there never was.

You check anyway. Twice, the first week.

There is sand in the turn-ups of the coat on the back of the door. You have not been to a beach. You take it to the window and turn it out over an ordinary carpet, and it is still there in the morning, and you leave it.

You eat alone, badly, standing up. Halfway through you find you have arranged what is on the plate — ten, then nine, then seven, and one laid across the whole of it — and there is no reason for it, and you do it again the following evening, and the evening after that.

Somewhere above you in this building a radio is playing, and it stops at eleven, and there is a person up there who turned it off. You have lived under them for a year. This morning that strikes you, for the first time in your life, as a thing that could be fixed.

The arithmetic stays with you longer than the town does. Two hundred people, each holding up their own eight feet of it, not one of them told what they were doing. You have started counting the people in this building. There are nine.

wake.furthermore:
Nothing. There is nothing behind the sternum and no warmth at the back of the neck and no enormous patience standing in the corner of anything.

You have your whole mind to yourself. It is very quiet in here.
wake.coda:
You went and got the language back, and it cost the town, and the town was made of you, and so was the cost.

Nobody is going to be able to tell you whether that was the right thing. Not because it is a hard question — because the only two people who could have argued it out are now one person, in an ordinary room, with a watch on the table that is going.

You will put the argument to yourself at intervals for the rest of your life. You will take both sides. You are extremely good at taking both sides; you have had eleven years of practice at it and you did not know that was what you were practising.

stay.title: and he does not
body:
You push the chair back toward him with your foot.

It is not a large gesture. It is not a gesture at all, particularly; it travels about eight inches across good boards and makes almost no sound doing it, and a man watching from the doorway would not have been able to say what had happened.

He looks at it for a while.

He looks at it for longer than eight inches of chair can reasonably require, with both hands still on the back of his own, and at no point does his face do any of the four things you have watched it do this evening.

"Right," he says. "Then I shall be careful."

And that is the entire acceptance, and it is the only promise anybody makes to anybody in this room tonight.

He sits down. It takes him a moment to do it, and the moment is not hesitation; it is a man sitting down in a chair he has not sat in for eleven years and finding that the height is wrong for him now.

He puts his hands on the machine. They are your hands with everything a sixteenth of an inch the other way — the same span, the same ink under the same nail, the callus on the wrong finger.

And he finishes the sentence.

You do not hear what he writes. You are not going to hear what he writes, ever, on any evening, in any town.

Because the thing about being described is that it is the least noticeable event available to a person. Nothing happens. Nothing has ever happened. It has been happening to you all your life at a rate of several thousand words a day and you have never once felt it land.

You come out of the seam somewhere in Silvora Reefs.

It is Durry Kwain, as it happens, and the bell over the door is still going, and Darek has the cone made, and there is a smear of blue on your coat that has not dried and never will.

"Sorry about your wait," he says.

And it lands. For the first time in eleven years the timing on that line is exactly, unremarkably right, and neither of you notices, and there is nothing to notice, and that is the whole of what has been arranged for you.

The rotors stop over the harbour that night and nobody mentions it, because nobody has ever mentioned them.

The count in the west corridor at Rest Assured settles at nineteen and stays there. The neon at Mary's says DUDE'S DEWS & DON'TS and goes on saying it. The hallway at Durry Kwain is eleven feet whether you walk it alone or not.

It is a good town. It has been made very carefully by somebody who has had eleven years of practice and two hundred drafts and one enormous piece of information about what it costs, and he is not going to waste it.

consequences.text: At the Outside Inn, a narrow man in a good coat is still two narrow men in the same good coat, and one of them raises a hand as you pass, and so does the other, and it is the wrong one, and neither of them minds.

At six o'clock every evening in a barbershop that cannot be directed to, an owlbear in an excellent coat addresses the empty air between the chairs, courteously, and is not answered, and does it again the following evening.

There is a new can on the shelf at Cheeses Thrice, at the near end, where the newest ones go.

It is labelled in a careful hand that has been getting steadier for some time: *The night he came in and asked what was in them.*

It holds. They all hold. Eleven years and forty-one cans and not one of them has gone vague, in a town where nothing else stays the shape it was put down in.

There are now twenty-three forms in a cupboard on a half-landing, all of them recommending that the resident not walk the west corridor alone after dark.

The twenty-third is in a hand that is not Landy's. It is filled in beautifully — every field complete, the language exactly right, the seal in the correct corner — and Landy files it without ever having written it, and does not appear to find that strange, and has not been asked to.

At Cheeses Thrice a joke dies on a Tuesday and the room repairs it — late, scattered, from four tables that did not look at each other — and the thickened patch over the third table thins and goes. Nobody remarks on it. Nobody ever has. It is the most reliable machine in the parish.

The vault at the end of the west corridor stands two fingers off its jamb. Soliloquy measures it every Michaelmas and it does not change, and she has stopped writing the number in the book, because she knows it, and because writing it down had begun to feel like a way of asking.

Ninety people a night arrange themselves across a floor at the Möbius and leave eight square feet clear in front of the far booth. Each of them has a sincere and different reason. Not one of them is right. It does not matter, and the shape holds.

In the third mirror at The G.'s Spot an owlbear turns, once, and thanks a pane of glass. The glass does not answer. It goes on including him, which it was always going to do, and which it has never once been asked to.

stay.furthermore:
He is still here. Of course he is still here.

He stands in the doorway of your flat with an unused saddle and infinite patience while you talk, and talk, and talk, and when the room has gone and there is only him left you turn and say '...and furthermore—'

And he listens. He always listens. That was never the part that was in doubt.
stay.coda:
You gave the last word away to the only other person alive who could have used it, and you got a town back, and everybody in it is going to be all right.

The decision will never be one you can point to afterwards. That is the shape of it: there is no moment in the record where you chose, because the choosing was done by a man who then stopped being the man who did it.

Somebody is being very careful with you. He is going to go on being very careful with you for a long time, and he is good at it, and you are never going to notice — and that is not a failure of yours. It is the whole of his craft, and he learned it on you.

together.title: Recommend company
body:
"Two chairs," you say. "You have kept two chairs in a room nine feet by eleven for eleven years, in which there was never going to be a visitor, and in which there was never going to be *room* for a visitor — and you have never once asked yourself why, because asking yourself why is my half of the job."

He does not answer that.

He sits down in his own chair, which he has not done all evening, and which he did not do in any of the two hundred drafts either, because in all of them he is standing at a wall when it happens.

And after a while — a considerable while, long enough for the lamp to be the only thing in the room doing anything — you sit down in the other one.

Nobody has ever sat in it. The cushion has not gone down anywhere. It takes your weight like new furniture.

The sentence gets finished by two people.

It takes a considerable amount of time. It is not a graceful process — he argues for a semicolon and you argue for letting the line breathe, and you argue about it for the better part of an hour in a room with no window and no clock and a cup with a ring under it older than the cup — and at some point during the argument the page in the machine acquires a second line, and neither of you can afterwards say who put it there.

That is the whole of the mechanism. That is what the entire fortnight has been walking toward and it is two men disagreeing about punctuation.

Silvora Reefs does not stop.

It does something much stranger, which is that it *settles*. The hallway at Durry Kwain finds a length and keeps it. The count in the west corridor comes out at nineteen twice running and Soliloquy, who has never in sixty years had a number come out twice running, stands very still in the middle of her own vestibule and does not say anything in couplets about it.

A snake on a sign outside a hanging building holds its coil. The ink on it dries. It has been wet for eleven years and it dries in about four minutes and nobody sees it happen.

The town goes on, and it goes on *held*.

Woolbinkle was right. That is a sentence nobody in this parish has ever had occasion to write down, and it should be written down somewhere it cannot go vague: if holding is possible here, then somebody had been choosing not to.

He worked that out behind a counter, alone, from forty cans and a bad history, and he was too polite to say the second half of it out loud to the man it was about.

It turns out the somebody was two people. Neither of them could do it alone — that part is not a moral, it is engineering, it was tested two hundred times in a basket by your foot.

And both of them had spent eleven years being perfectly certain that the failure was a failure of will.

consequences.text: Monsieur Albert is mentioned. Frequently, by name, in the room, by two writers who have a great deal of catching up to do on the subject of who is in it. He comes out of the glass over about nine months. He is not graceful about it and he does not care.

At the Outside Inn, Dee Stroii is asked — properly, with a chair, over a considerable period — which of him would like to be the one. He declines to choose. He has grown fond of the arrangement and he would like it noted that nobody ever asked before.

Bud Onkuhdonk keeps saying it is a light well. He is told, once, gently, by a man in a good coat, that he can stop. He does not stop. He has a system and the building has stood for nine years and he is not about to run an experiment.

Asimov Sobeleaux measures his corridor with a tape, alone, on a Tuesday, and gets the same answer he got on Monday.

He measures it again on the Wednesday, because a man does not accept a thing like that on two readings. Same answer.

Then he goes and sits down in his office among the charts of waterways that appear on no map, for rather a long time, without turning any of them over.

Lying Landy mends the trestle.

It takes an afternoon and he will not be helped and he will not be watched, and when it is done the leg is a leg and the desk stands level and there is no shim in it.

The shim comes out. It is put in a plastic wallet and the wallet goes into an inside pocket over the heart, where it lives, and where it is going to go on living — and the leg does not come back, and the form in the wallet is never filed.

The drain on the Möbius ice machine runs downhill. Ginny finds it on a Tuesday, on her knees, with two fingers, and swears at eleven inches of pipe for a considerable time, and then sits down on the floor of her own cellar and laughs until she has to stop.

The volume of air between the two chairs at The G.'s Spot is air. Antonio walks through it forty times a day and arrives exactly when he arrives, and Monsieur Albert, who is in the room now and takes some getting used to, has opinions about the coffee.

Woolbinkle tells somebody about the cans. Not you — a woman who comes in on a Thursday for a nine-inch and asks, on the way in rather than on the way out, what is on the shelf. He is ready. He has been ready for eleven years.

Ben has the masks rehung. It takes four days and he will not be helped and he will not say why. When it is done every sightline in the room converges on the middle of the long side, and he sits down in it, with his palms flat, and lets them look at him.

Soliloquy signs a delivery docket H. O'Dochtaigh.

In her own hand, without deciding to, at the door, with a man waiting for the clipboard back — for the first time since 1961.

And then she stands in the vestibule looking at it for rather a long while afterwards, with the horizontal behind her and the parish below, not saying anything at all in a building where she has said something every day for sixty years.

together.furthermore:
He puts his head round the door of a room that has no door, which he has been doing for as long as you have had a skull, and he looks at the two of you arguing about a semicolon.

Then he draws himself up. The air thickens. Something vast is being assembled behind his soft eyes, something that has been waiting since before there were words to wait in—

"Finally," he says, and goes to sleep in the corner.
together.coda:
Neither of you got the last word.

That was the arrangement, and it took a fortnight and two hundred drafts and a shim in a table leg to arrive at, and neither of you would have accepted it on the first evening or the tenth.

It is the only outcome in which the man with the ice cream is still standing behind his counter, running a touch previous, apologising for a wait that has never happened to anybody.

The remedy was never available. That is the thing the form got right, in a hand better than Landy's, eleven years ago, under a heading nobody ever read: *none available.* And underneath it, in the same careful hand, the part that turned out to be the whole of it. *Recommend company.*

nevermind.title: Nevermind
body:
—say.

And he says it.

Not the word. He has been not-saying the word for as long as you have had a mind for him to not-say it in — since a kitchen, since before the kitchen, since before there was anything in you organised enough to be disappointed.

And every single time the build has been enormous. The air thickens, something vast assembles itself behind those soft eyes, the whole room leans in — and then one flat syllable, delivered without emphasis, letting all the air out at once.

You have loved him for it and been maddened by it in roughly equal measure for forty-four years, and you could not now say which of the two has done more to keep you upright.

This time he finishes the sentence.

It is not in words. He is older than language and he has always regarded it as a fad, and he is not going to take it up now at the last minute for the convenience of two men in a small room.

It arrives as weight, and as warmth at the back of the neck, and as the particular pressure behind the sternum that you have been calling him since you were eight years old, and it is perfectly, unmistakably, unambiguously clear, and it is this:

*You have both been in here talking to yourselves. I have been in here the whole time. Somebody has been listening. That was never the part that was in doubt.*

Revilo sits down on the floor.

Not the chair. He has two chairs in this room and he goes past both of them and puts himself on the boards, with his back against a wall that is a window, in a green tailcoat with purple accents, in a room he has not left in eleven years.

He does it slowly, the way a much older man sits down.

And he puts his head back against the wall, and looks up at a ceiling he wrote himself — every joist of it, the stain in the corner, the picture rail nobody ever hung anything from — and says:

"I have been so *lonely*, and there has been an elephant."

The page in the machine is not finished by either of you.

It is not finished at all. It is taken out, carefully, by four hands, and folded twice, and put in a plastic wallet in an inside pocket over the heart where it lives — and the sentence stays in the present continuous, unresolved, fraying gently, exactly the way this town has always run.

Silvora Reefs was never being held together by an author. It was being held together by somebody being listened to. It has been over-engineered for a decade and it turns out the load-bearing element was an irrelevant elephant with an unused saddle who never once left.

consequences.text: The whispers at Rest Assured resolve, finally, into forty voices in your cadence, and what they are all saying, in the careful grammar of overheard speech that is not overheard speech, is: '...and furthermore—'

Nobody writes anything for a fortnight.

The town does not stop. The queue moves, the squeegee arcs, the oven comes up to temperature at four and holds it. Nothing goes vague, nothing frays, nothing requires attention.

The town has never once needed it continuously, and both of them spend that fortnight finding that out — in bars, at length, badly, and with a certain amount of shouting in the street at two in the morning about whose fault the last eleven years were.

There are two of you in the Outside Inn on a Thursday, in a green coat and a purple one, under thirty feet of indoor weather.

You are being served by a bellhop who begins every response with BUT and who has never in his life been so profoundly relieved to have two of something to deny at once — because two is a category, and a category can be handled, and BUT there's two of you is a sentence that does considerably more work than BUT there's one.

In the kitchen at Lishush Mush the pass goes light during a long sentence, and six things come up, and they stay up a good deal longer than they used to. T has stopped apologising for it. T has started writing longer sentences.

T signs for a delivery in a hurry, with a knife still in his other hand and the pass going behind him: one clean stroke, the mark a man makes who cannot write his name.

The driver witnesses it without looking up. It stands. It goes into a book in a van and out of the parish and nobody ever queries it, and it has always stood, and it was always going to.

Soliloquy puts it down. She tells the whole of it to a bellhop who begins every sentence with BUT, in a vestibule, at four in the afternoon — and he denies every word of it, warmly, at length, for an hour and a half, and she goes back inside lighter than she has been since 1961.

Nothing is finished. The sentence in the machine stays in the present continuous and frays gently at the edge and does not come apart, because fraying is only fatal to a thing that is on its own — and there are two men in that room now, and an elephant, and the elephant has never once been in a hurry.

nevermind.furthermore:
Nevermind.

He says it afterwards. He says it about six weeks afterwards, in a completely ordinary moment, after no build-up whatsoever, apropos of nothing, in the middle of a Tuesday — and it is the funniest thing that has ever happened to anybody, and you laugh until you have to sit down on a kerb outside a shop that sells dews and don'ts.
nevermind.coda:
The sentence never got finished and nobody kept the language.

And the whole apparatus — the countdown cut into brass by hand, the Coalition and its four-lobed cards, the forty vaults settled in advance, the eleven years of somebody being extremely careful about a man who did not know he was being kept — turned out to be two halves of one person not talking to each other.

In front of a witness. Who had been standing in the room the entire time, older than language and unimpressed by it, waiting for one of them to stop making a case long enough for somebody else to say something.

He waited since before either of them could speak. He was never once in a hurry about it. That was the point, and it took forty-four years and a purple elephant to make it, and it was made in the end without a single word.
